s0001: Explain how an animal's behavior in danger helps it survive
s0002: Look at exactly what the animal does when it is in danger and think about how this protects it from enemies; rule out facts that have nothing to do with the behavior or that are wrong.
s0003:
The desert tortoise lives in the deserts and foothills of Uzbekistan. It has a hard shell on its back. When it senses danger, the tortoise pulls its head and legs inside its shell.
How does this behavior help the tortoise?
s0004: The tortoise can run away faster.
s0006: The tortoise's soft body parts are protected inside the hard shell.
s0007: The tortoise makes itself look like another animal.
s0008: Danger → head and legs inside the shell
s0009: When a tortoise senses danger, it pulls its head and legs inside its shell.
s0010: Head and legs — soft; shell — hard
s0011: The head and legs are soft and easy to bite. The shell, however, is very hard.
s0012: An enemy cannot bite through the hard shell
s0013: Once the soft parts are hidden in the shell, an enemy cannot reach them.
s0014: Answer: C) the soft parts are protected
s0015: So the correct answer is C.
s0016: A student who chose A did not think about the purpose of the behavior: a tortoise with its legs pulled in cannot walk at all.
s0017: A student who chose B confused the tortoise with animals that puff themselves up when in danger; a tortoise does not get bigger when it goes into its shell.
s0018: A student who chose D confused camouflage with protection; hiding in its shell does not make the tortoise look like another animal.
s0019: Think about which parts of the tortoise are soft and which part is hard.
s0020:
If an enemy grabs a lizard by its tail, the lizard drops its tail and runs away. The tail that has come off keeps wriggling on the ground for a while.
How does this behavior help the lizard?
s0021: The enemy is distracted by the wriggling tail, and the lizard escapes.
s0022: Without its tail, the lizard looks bigger to the enemy.
s0023: The dropped tail poisons the enemy.
s0024: The enemy cannot see a lizard without a tail in the sand.
s0025: Enemy grabs the tail → the tail comes off
s0026: If an enemy catches a lizard by its tail, the tail breaks off.
s0027: Tail wriggles → the enemy looks at it
s0028: The dropped tail keeps wriggling and draws the enemy's attention.
s0030: While the enemy is busy with the tail, the lizard escapes.
s0031: Answer: A) the enemy is distracted, the lizard escapes
s0032: So the correct answer is A.
s0033: A student who chose B did not take into account that a lizard gets smaller when it loses its tail; it does not look bigger.
s0034: A student who chose C confused the lizard with poisonous animals; there is no poison in its tail.
s0035: A student who chose D linked the tail to hiding; a lizard without a tail can still be seen, and it gets away only by running.
s0036: Imagine what the enemy does when it sees the wriggling tail.

s0049: A scorpion's body is covered on the outside with a hard covering, and it has no bones inside.

s0165: Connect desert animals being active at night with adapting to the scorching daytime heat
s0166: Remember how day and night differ in the desert (temperature, moisture) and think about how an animal avoids the most dangerous conditions.
s0167:
In the Kyzylkum Desert, many animals, such as jerboas, gerbils and long-eared hedgehogs, stay in their burrows during the day and look for food at night.
Why are many desert animals more active at night?
s0168: The air is drier at night.
s0169: Food is easier to see by moonlight at night.
s0170: There is no wind at night.
s0171: The air is cooler at night.
s0172: Desert in summer, daytime: very hot
s0173: In summer in the Kyzylkum, the air gets very hot during the day, and the sand gets even hotter.
s0175: After the Sun sets, the desert air cools down quickly.
s0176: In the cool, an animal loses less water
s0177: When it is cool, an animal does not overheat and loses less water from its body.
s0178: Answer: D) it is cooler at night
s0179: A student who chose A thought the opposite: in the desert, the air at night is not drier than in the daytime but a little more humid.
s0180: A student who chose B thought night is brighter; even with the Moon, night is darker than day.
s0181: A student who chose C thought there is no wind in the desert at night; the wind can blow at night too — the main difference is the temperature.
s0182: Compare what the air is like in the desert during the day and at night.
s0183:
In summer in the Kyzylkum, the sand gets so hot during the day that you cannot step on it barefoot. A jerboa stays in its deep burrow during the day and comes out after sunset.

s0185: It is protected from the scorching daytime heat.

s0191: Underground, in a deep burrow, the temperature is much lower.
s0192: Night: cool outside → it comes out

s0195: A student who chose A thought the burrow is a storeroom; the jerboa looks for food outside at night.
s0196: A student who chose C thought it rains in the desert at night; in summer it hardly ever rains in the desert.
s0197: A student who chose D thought the wind gives an animal strength; an animal gets its strength from food.
s0198: Think about what the temperature is like outside during the day and inside a deep burrow.

s0204: Calcium helps the eyes see well.

s0229: Put the three states of water (ice, liquid water, steam) in order by temperature
s0230: Remember that ice forms when water freezes (0 °C and below), and steam forms when water boils (around 100 °C); the temperature of liquid water is in between.
s0231:
Ice, water and steam have different temperatures.
Which order goes correctly from HOTTEST TO COLDEST?
s0237: Steam comes out of a boiling kettle; it is the hottest.
s0239: Ice forms when water freezes; it is the coldest.
s0241: Liquid water is warmer than ice and colder than steam.
s0243: So from hottest to coldest: steam, water, ice. The correct answer is C.
s0244: A student who chose A knew the order but read the question too quickly and wrote it from coldest to hottest.
s0245: A student who chose B thought water is hotter than steam; in fact, steam forms when water boils and is hotter than water.
s0246: A student who chose D thought ice is warmer than water; ice forms when water cools down and freezes.

s0339: Use the result of an experiment (the pulling distance) to compare the strength of two magnets with good reasons
s0340: Check that the experiment is fair (the same object, the same table), then look at the result: the stronger magnet pulls the object from farther away. What matters is the result of the experiment, not the size or color of the magnet.
s0341:
Sardor has two magnets (1 and 2) and two identical iron nails.
On a table, he slowly moved each magnet toward a nail. Magnet 1 pulled the nail from a distance of 12 cm, but magnet 2 pulled it only from 6 cm.
Dilshod said, “Both magnets are equally strong.” Which answer is correct?
s0342: Yes, Dilshod is right, because both magnets pulled the nail.
s0343: No, magnet 1 is stronger, because it pulled the nail from farther away.
s0344: No, magnet 2 is stronger, because it waited until the nail was closer.
s0345: Yes, Dilshod is right, because the nails are identical.
s0346: The experiment is fair: same nails, same table
s0347: The same kind of nail and the same table were used for both magnets.
s0349: The first magnet pulled the nail from twelve centimeters, and the second from six centimeters.
s0351: The magnet that could pull the nail from farther away is stronger.
s0352: Answer: B) no, magnet 1 is stronger
s0353: So Dilshod is not right. The correct answer is B.
s0354: A student who chose A only looked at whether the magnets pulled the nail at all and did not compare the pulling distances.
s0355: A student who chose C drew the opposite conclusion: a magnet that pulls the nail only from closer up is weaker.
s0356: A student who chose D mistook the fairness of the experiment for its result; the nails are the same, but the magnets' results are different.
s0357: Compare which magnet could pull the nail from farther away.
s0358:
Zuhra has a red magnet and a blue magnet. The red magnet is bigger than the blue magnet.

s0362: Both magnets are equally strong, because both of them pulled the clip.
s0364: The same clip and the same table were used for both magnets — the experiment is fair.
s0366: The red magnet pulled the clip from four centimeters, and the blue magnet from nine centimeters.
s0368: The magnet that pulls from farther away is stronger. The size of the magnet does not matter here.

s0370: A student who chose A looked at the size of the magnet, not at the result of the experiment; a small magnet can be stronger.
s0371: A student who chose B understood the distance the wrong way around: pulling only from closer up is a sign of weakness.

s0374: Apply the link between weight and distance from the pivot to balance a seesaw
s0375: Children of the same weight balance when they sit the same distance from the pivot. A child who is twice as heavy must sit twice as close to the pivot.

In each picture, the top shows Bobur and Zarina, and the bottom shows Bobur and Sherzod. In which picture is the seesaw balanced in both cases?
s0384: Bobur = Zarina → both at the ends
s0385: Bobur and Zarina weigh the same, so they must sit the same distance from the pivot.
s0387: Sherzod is twice as heavy as Bobur.
s0388: Heavier child → closer to the pivot (halfway)
s0389: The heavier child sits closer to the pivot: if Bobur is at the end, Sherzod sits halfway.
s0390: Fig. 4: top, both at the ends; bottom, Sherzod nearer the middle
s0391: That is exactly what the fourth picture shows.
s0393: A student who chose A (Fig. 1) did not take weight into account: if Sherzod also sits at the end, the seesaw tips toward his side.
s0394: A student who chose B (Fig. 2) thought the opposite: they moved the lighter Bobur closer and put the heavier Sherzod at the end.
s0395: A student who chose C (Fig. 3) got Sherzod right but also moved Zarina, who weighs the same as Bobur, closer to the pivot.
